Gratuitous

gruh-TOO-uh-tus -- from Latin gratuitus, 'free, given as a favor,' from gratia, 'favor, kindness': something gratuitous is given without being asked for. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Gratuitous is uncalled for and unwarranted.

The critic complained that the play's extra twenty minutes of unrelated dance numbers felt entirely gratuitous.

Worked Example

The coach added an extra, unannounced lap around the field purely to make an example of the one player who had arrived two minutes late.

Gratuitous describes something added without real justification, often just to make a point or for effect -- an extra lap that punishes the whole team for one late arrival serves no real training purpose beyond making an example.

How Gratuitous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

needless

needless: not needed; unnecessary

unwarranted

unwarranted: not justified or appropriate given the situation

Antonyms

justified

justified: shown to be right or reasonable

necessary

necessary: required; needed

How Strong Is It? — needless → gratuitous → unwarranted

needless vs. gratuitous

needless vs. gratuitous: Needless is a plain, everyday word for anything unnecessary, while gratuitous adds a sharper criticism that something was added deliberately and inappropriately.

unwarranted vs. gratuitous

unwarranted vs. gratuitous: Unwarranted goes a step further than gratuitous by emphasizing that something wasn't just unnecessary but actively lacked any real justification.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — grat-

root — grat-: pleasing, thankful, given as a favor (Latin gratia)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Gratuitous comes from Latin gratuitus, 'given freely, without payment,' from gratia, 'favor or kindness' -- something gratuitous was originally just 'given for free,' the same root behind the word gratitude.
